title: Envy (Avot 4:21)
hookLine: envy, desire and honor-seeking drive a person from the world

cards: A thumb scrolls. Someone's new kitchen, all white marble. Someone's promotion, with a long string of congratulations underneath.
Someone's beach. Nothing bad has happened. The day was fine a minute ago.

And yet something shifts in the chest, a small sour pull, and the fine day looks a little smaller than it did. Pirkei Avot names that pull alongside two companions, and says what the three of them do to a person.

teach.h: ENVY, DESIRE, HONOR: OUT OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Kin'ah. Envy. Turn it four ways.
First, the saying. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches in Pirkei Avot: envy, desire, and the chase after honor drive a person out of the world. You met a cousin of that line long ago, with the good eye.
Readers take out of the world more than one way. Some hear it about this life: an envious person can stand somewhere beautiful and not be there at all, their attention always next door.
Others hear it about the world to come. Both agree envy takes something from the one who feels it. Second, the body.
Proverbs, in the King James words: "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones." The damage isn't placed in the person envied. They're on the beach.
It's in the one holding it, slowly. Third, a surprise.

In tractate Bava Batra, the Talmud has a kind word for one kind of kin'ah: the envy of scholars increases wisdom. Seeing a classmate learn more can push you to study harder. So the same word can name a rot or a spur.
The difference seems to lie in direction: wanting the other person to have less, or reaching for more yourself. Fourth, the way back. Ten days ago this path heard Ben Zoma on honor.
His question just before it fits here: who is rich?
The one who is happy with their portion.
Not the one with the most. The one who can see what's on their own table. That's the opposite of being driven out of the world.

how: Jews study Pirkei Avot, including Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's teaching on envy and Ben Zoma's 'who is rich'; Mussar students often take envy as a trait to work on, alongside gratitude for one's portion.

o: envy, which can rot you or spur you on
anger that flares up all at once

p: envy, desire, honor: out of the world
envy, the rottenness of the bones
rich is happy with their portion

s: envy mainly harms the person envied
Proverbs pictures it in the envier's own bones; the envied are on the beach.
the Talmud finds one kind of envy useful
Bava Batra says the envy of scholars increases wisdom.
Avot says the rich are those with the most
Ben Zoma: the rich are those happy with their portion.

games.q: your study partner is learning faster than you, and you feel the sting. which kind of kin'ah does the Talmud praise?
o: letting it push you to study harder.
games.why: Bava Batra says the envy of scholars increases wisdom: envy that makes you reach for more, not wish the other less.

practice: Name one person you've envied lately; nobody else is listening.
Ask which kind it is: if it points at something you'd like to grow toward, keep the direction and drop the sourness, and if it wants them to have less, set it down like a bag carried too long.
Then name three real, ordinary things on your own table, and if you pray, give thanks for your portion in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Kin'ah. Envy. Avot names it among the things that drive a person out of the world, though the Talmud allows that the envy of scholars can increase wisdom. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: envy or jealousy; the same word can also mean zeal.

carryVoice: Your line: envy removes. Your own table is still there to see. Until next time.

sources.q: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
